items.stem: ‘Technological invention was the main cause of the Industrial Revolution.’ How far do you agree?
items.answer: For: Machines such as the water frame and mule transformed cotton production. Watt's steam engine made power available away from rivers. Coke smelting and puddling allowed mass production of iron. Against: Population growth provided labour and a home market. Agricultural improvement fed the towns. Capital from trade and stable government financed industry. Inventions were a response to demand, high wages and cheap coal. Judgement: invention was the visible driver of change, but it depended on the demand, capital and resources that made new machines profitable.

items.stem: ‘The railways were the most important economic development in Britain between 1750 and 1850.’ Discuss.
items.answer: For: They transformed transport costs and speeds. They created demand for coal, iron and engineering. They linked national markets and stimulated investment. Against: Railways came late; most growth before 1830 came from cotton, iron and canals. Cotton was the leading sector and largest export. Steam power underpinned both factories and railways. Judgement: railways were transformative after 1830, but for most of the period the cotton industry and steam power were more important.

items.stem: ‘Industrialisation made life worse for most working people before 1850.’ How far do you agree with this view?
items.answer: For: Overcrowded, insanitary towns raised death rates. Factory work brought long hours, strict discipline and child labour. Groups such as handloom weavers suffered falling earnings. Against: Many estimates show real wages rising after about 1820. Cheaper cotton clothing and goods became available. Factory work offered more regular employment than farm labour. Experience varied greatly by region, trade and decade. Judgement: for many urban workers conditions worsened before 1840, but the picture was mixed and improvements in wages began before 1850.

items.stem: ‘Chartism failed mainly because of the divisions within the movement.’ Discuss.
items.answer: For: Moral and physical force leaders such as Lovett and O'Connor quarrelled. Regional and local differences weakened national organisation. The Newport Rising of 1839 alienated moderate opinion. Against: Parliament had no intention of conceding democracy. Government repression and the army were effective. Economic recovery after 1842 and 1848 reduced support. Middle-class reformers were absorbed by the Anti-Corn Law League. Judgement: divisions weakened Chartism, but the decisive reason was the refusal of a Parliament elected on a narrow franchise to concede, backed by the power of the state.

items.stem: To what extent was agricultural change a necessary precondition for industrialisation?
items.answer: For: Higher output fed a growing urban population. Rising farm incomes created demand for manufactured goods. Enclosure and improvement released some labour for industry. Against: Much of the industrial labour force came from natural population growth. Capital came mainly from trade and industry itself. Coal, technology and overseas markets were more direct causes. Judgement: agricultural change was an important support but not a precondition on its own; it worked together with population growth and trade.

items.answer: Source C: Smith argues that the division of labour is the main cause of increased productivity. Source D: It suggests that machinery hugely increased output and that profits were reinvested. A similarity and a difference must each be supported by details from both sources.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a similarity and 1 for supporting it from both sources; 1 mark for a difference and 1 for supporting it from both sources [4]

items.stem: What is meant by “puddling”?
options: Henry Cort's process of 1784 for making wrought iron by stirring molten pig iron in a reverberatory furnace.
The belief that government should interfere as little as possible in economic and social life.
A body that maintained a stretch of road and charged tolls for its use.
A parliamentary seat with very few voters, often controlled by a patron.
items.answer: Henry Cort's process of 1784 for making wrought iron by stirring molten pig iron in a reverberatory furnace.
items.markingKey: Puddling: Henry Cort's process of 1784 for making wrought iron by stirring molten pig iron in a reverberatory furnace. [1]

items.stem: Which of these events happened first?
options: Henry Cort patented the puddling process
Watt's engine was adapted to produce rotary motion
The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened
items.answer: Watt's engine was adapted to produce rotary motion
items.markingKey: Watt's engine was adapted to produce rotary motion (1781); Henry Cort patented the puddling process (1784); Cartwright designed the power loom (1785); the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened (1830). [1]

items.stem: Consider the following explanations of why railways had such a large economic impact by 1850. A: They cut the cost and time of moving goods and people. B: They attracted large-scale investment through joint-stock companies. C: They opened national markets for goods such as fresh food. Explain which of these was the most important reason.
items.answer: Any reasoned choice. A: They cut the cost and time of moving goods and people. B: They attracted large-scale investment through joint-stock companies. C: They opened national markets for goods such as fresh food. Possible judgement: their greatest impact was in creating demand for heavy industry and in linking national markets.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a choice; up to 3 marks for explaining it with precise detail; up to 2 marks for comparing it with the other reasons [6]

items.stem: How far did the Industrial Revolution change the British economy by 1850?
items.answer: For: Factory production dominated cotton. Output of coal and iron rose many times over. A national railway network existed. Against: Agriculture was still the largest single employer. Many industries such as building and clothing used traditional methods. Workshop and domestic production remained common. Judgement: key sectors were transformed, but in 1850 much of the economy still worked in traditional ways.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (18-20): sustained analysis of both sides of the question, supported by precise evidence, with a well-substantiated judgement. Level 4 (15-17): developed analysis of both sides; a judgement is reached but is not fully supported. Level 3 (10-14): analysis of one side, or of both with limited development or accuracy. Level 2 (6-9): mainly descriptive, with implicit links to the question. Level 1 (1-5): general assertions with little accurate knowledge. Agree / supporting: Factory production dominated cotton. Output of coal and iron rose many times over. A national railway network existed. Disagree / other factors: Agriculture was still the largest single employer. Many industries such as building and clothing used traditional methods. Workshop and domestic production remained common. Possible judgement: key sectors were transformed, but in 1850 much of the economy still worked in traditional ways. [20]

items.stem: Which of these events happened last?
options: Engels published The Condition of the Working Class in England
items.answer: Engels published The Condition of the Working Class in England
items.markingKey: Engels published The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845); the Luddite machine-breaking began (1811); the Peterloo Massacre took place (1819); the Tolpuddle Martyrs were transported (1834). [1]

items.stem: Cholera struck British towns in 1831-32 and again in 1848-49. Explain why living conditions in industrial towns were so poor in the 1830s and 1840s.
items.answer: Towns grew too fast for housing and services to keep up. Builders put up cheap back-to-backs and cellar dwellings. There was little clean water or sewerage, so diseases such as cholera and typhus spread. Local government was weak and laissez-faire ideas discouraged spending. Low wages left families in overcrowded rooms. Judgement: rapid growth was the root cause, but weak local government and laissez-faire attitudes explain why problems were left unsolved.
items.markingKey: Level 4 (9-10): explains a range of causes and reaches a supported judgement about their relative importance or how they are linked. Level 3 (6-8): explains two or more causes; any judgement is undeveloped. Level 2 (3-5): describes or identifies causes, or explains only one. Level 1 (1-2): general, unsupported points. Indicative content: Towns grew too fast for housing and services to keep up. Builders put up cheap back-to-backs and cellar dwellings. There was little clean water or sewerage, so diseases such as cholera and typhus spread. Local government was weak and laissez-faire ideas discouraged spending. Low wages left families in overcrowded rooms. Possible judgement: rapid growth was the root cause, but weak local government and laissez-faire attitudes explain why problems were left unsolved. [10]

items.stem: A revision guide lists these reasons why a sense of working-class identity developed by the 1830s. A: Movements such as trade unions and the radical press spread ideas. B: Events such as Peterloo created common grievances. C: Exclusion from the vote by the 1832 Reform Act. Explain which of these was the most important reason.
items.answer: Any reasoned choice. A: Movements such as trade unions and the radical press spread ideas. B: Events such as Peterloo created common grievances. C: Exclusion from the vote by the 1832 Reform Act. Possible judgement: shared conditions created the potential, but political exclusion after 1832 turned it into a sense of class.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a choice; up to 3 marks for explaining it with precise detail; up to 2 marks for comparing it with the other reasons [6]

items.stem: Put these events in chronological order, starting with the earliest. A: The first Public Health Act was passed. B: The People's Charter was published. C: The Great Reform Act was passed. D: The Factory Act banned children under nine from textile mills.
items.markingKey: Correct order C, D, B, A (C 1832; D 1833; B 1838; A 1848): 2 marks if all correct, 1 mark if one adjacent pair is reversed. [2]

items.stem: Isla is planning an answer to the question: “‘Chartism failed mainly because of the divisions within the movement.’ How far do you agree?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Isla could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: divisions weakened Chartism, but the decisive reason was the refusal of a Parliament elected on a narrow franchise to concede, backed by the power of the state. Support: Moral and physical force leaders such as Lovett and O'Connor quarrelled. Regional and local differences weakened national organisation. Challenge: Parliament had no intention of conceding democracy. Government repression and the army were effective.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: Historians have offered several reasons why Chartism failed to achieve its aims by 1848. A: The middle classes supported the Anti-Corn Law League instead. B: Parliament rejected all three petitions. C: The authorities used troops, police and arrests effectively. Which was the most significant? Explain your answer with reference to the other reasons.
items.answer: Any reasoned choice. A: The middle classes supported the Anti-Corn Law League instead. B: Parliament rejected all three petitions. C: The authorities used troops, police and arrests effectively. Possible judgement: Parliament's refusal and the strength of the state were decisive, but divisions and dependence on economic distress weakened the movement.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a choice; up to 3 marks for explaining it with precise detail; up to 2 marks for comparing it with the other reasons [6]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this description: “the organisation of production in workers' homes, with merchants supplying raw materials and collecting finished goods”.
items.answer: Domestic system
items.markingKey: Domestic system: the organisation of production in workers' homes, with merchants supplying raw materials and collecting finished goods. [1]

items.stem: Which of these statements is accurate?
options: Enclosure helped farmers adopt new methods such as crop rotation.
Steam power had replaced water power in most textile mills by 1800.
The 1832 Reform Act gave the vote to most working men.
Britain's first national census was taken in 1851.
items.answer: Enclosure helped farmers adopt new methods such as crop rotation.
items.markingKey: Compact holdings made it easier to experiment and to improve land. The other statements are inaccurate. [1]

items.stem: Freya is planning an answer to the question: “‘Technological invention was the main cause of the Industrial Revolution.’ How far do you agree?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Freya could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: invention was the visible driver of change, but it depended on the demand, capital and resources that made new machines profitable. Support: Machines such as the water frame and mule transformed cotton production. Watt's steam engine made power available away from rivers. Challenge: Population growth provided labour and a home market. Agricultural improvement fed the towns.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: Read the sources carefully. Source A: a report on a cotton mill by a visitor, 1790s (illustrative). “One machine, turned by water, now does the work that two hundred women spinning at home once did. The master tells me his profits are laid out each year in more machines.” Source B: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, 1776 (opening of Book I, abridged). “The greatest improvement in the productive powers of labour ... seem to have been the effects of the division of labour.” “Technological invention was the main cause of the Industrial Revolution.” How far do Sources A and B support this view?
items.answer: Source A supports: it shows machinery transforming production. Evaluation: the visitor relies on the mill owner's own claims. Source B challenges: it stresses organisation of work rather than invention. Evaluation: he was writing before the factory system and steam power were widespread. Grouping: support A; challenge B. A judgement must weigh how convincing each group is, using provenance and own knowledge, rather than counting sources.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): evaluates the sources (provenance, purpose, context, cross-reference) to show how far they support AND challenge the view, reaching a supported judgement. Level 4 (13-16): uses the sources to support AND challenge the view and evaluates some of them. Level 3 (9-12): uses the sources at face value to support AND challenge. Level 2 (5-8): uses the sources to support OR challenge. Level 1 (1-4): writes about the topic without valid use of the sources. (The examination version uses four sources and 25 marks; levels are scaled.) [20]

items.stem: What is meant by “turnpike trust”?
options: Henry Cort's process of 1784 for making wrought iron by stirring molten pig iron in a reverberatory furnace.
A body that maintained a stretch of road and charged tolls for its use.
The turning motion produced by Watt's engines after 1781, which allowed steam to drive factory machinery.
The growth of towns and the movement of people from the countryside into them.
items.answer: A body that maintained a stretch of road and charged tolls for its use.
items.markingKey: Turnpike trust: a body that maintained a stretch of road and charged tolls for its use. [1]

items.stem: Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: Steam power had replaced water power in most textile mills by 1800.
Britain's first national census was taken in 1851.
Canals were faster than railways for carrying passengers.
Railway building increased demand for coal and iron.
items.answer: Railway building increased demand for coal and iron.
items.markingKey: Rails, locomotives and bridges used vast amounts of iron, and engines burned coal. The other statements are inaccurate. [1]

items.stem: Diego is planning an answer to the question: “‘The railways were the most important economic development in Britain between 1750 and 1850.’ How far do you agree?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Diego could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: railways were transformative after 1830, but for most of the period the cotton industry and steam power were more important. Support: They transformed transport costs and speeds. They created demand for coal, iron and engineering. Challenge: Railways came late; most growth before 1830 came from cotton, iron and canals. Cotton was the leading sector and largest export.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: Study all the sources. Source A: a speech by a Manchester merchant, 1830s (illustrative). “Goods that took a week by canal now reach Liverpool in a day. Our trade has never been so brisk, and every foundry in the district is busy making rails and engines.” Source B: a historian writing in 1985 (illustrative). “The railways were the child of industrialisation, not its parent. By 1830 the cotton industry was already Britain's greatest export and steam had been at work for half a century.” How far do Sources A and B support the view that the railways were the most important economic development of the period?
items.answer: Source A supports: it presents railways as transforming trade and industry. Evaluation: he is an enthusiast who may exaggerate the benefits. Source B challenges: it argues cotton and steam mattered earlier and more. Evaluation: it is one historian's interpretation. Grouping: support A; challenge B. A judgement must weigh how convincing each group is, using provenance and own knowledge, rather than counting sources.

items.stem: Which of these statements is accurate?
options: Real wages fell steadily and sharply for all workers between 1780 and 1850.
Most of the capital for early textile mills came from large London banks.
All six points of the Charter had been achieved by 1850.
Chadwick's report linked poor sanitation with disease and early death.
items.answer: Chadwick's report linked poor sanitation with disease and early death.

items.stem: Explain why a sense of working-class identity developed by the 1830s.
items.answer: Shared experience of factory discipline and long hours. Concentration of workers in towns made organisation easier. Exclusion from the vote by the 1832 Reform Act. Movements such as trade unions and the radical press spread ideas. Events such as Peterloo created common grievances. Judgement: shared conditions created the potential, but political exclusion after 1832 turned it into a sense of class.

Level 3 (6-8): explains two or more causes; any judgement is undeveloped. Level 2 (3-5): describes or identifies causes, or explains only one. Level 1 (1-2): general, unsupported points. items.stem: Amara is planning an answer to the question: “‘Industrialisation made life worse for most working people before 1850.’ How far do you agree?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Amara could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: for many urban workers conditions worsened before 1840, but the picture was mixed and improvements in wages began before 1850. Support: Overcrowded, insanitary towns raised death rates. Factory work brought long hours, strict discipline and child labour. Challenge: Many estimates show real wages rising after about 1820. Cheaper cotton clothing and goods became available.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: A student writes: “The 1832 Reform Act gave the vote to most working men.” Is this accurate? Explain your answer using your own knowledge.
items.answer: Not accurate. It enfranchised mainly the middle class; only about one adult man in five in England and Wales could vote afterwards.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a correct judgement; 1 mark for accurate supporting knowledge [2]

items.stem: Grace is planning an answer to the question: “How far did governments respond effectively to the social problems caused by industrialisation by 1850?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Grace could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: governments began to accept a role in social reform, but by 1850 the response was limited and piecemeal. Support: Factory Acts of 1833, 1844 and 1847 limited hours for children and women. The Mines Act of 1842 banned women and young children underground. Challenge: Most laws were limited and weakly enforced. Local boards of health were voluntary unless death rates were very high.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: Read Source D. The Charter demanded a vote for every man over twenty-one, the secret ballot, no property qualification for MPs, payment of MPs, equal constituencies and annual parliaments. (The People's Charter, 1838 (summary of its six points).) How reliable is Source D as evidence about Chartist aims? Use the provenance of the source and your own knowledge.
items.answer: Reliable because it is the founding document of the movement. Less reliable because it shows aims, not how much support or unity the movement had. Cross-reference: It does not show how Chartists planned to achieve these aims. Judgement: reliable as evidence of this point of view, but it needs to be tested against other evidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point about the content; up to 2 marks for using the provenance (author, date, purpose, audience) to judge reliability; up to 2 marks for cross-referencing with own knowledge; 1 mark for a supported overall judgement [6]
